title: The One With Rachels New Dress

jokes.text: It is true what they say: Pregnant bellies look like a drum.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is visibly pregnant and playing music — audience expects a comment about pregnancy or music separately.
jokes.punchline: She conflates the two observations as if 'pregnant bellies look like a drum' is a universal truism everyone knows.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe logic — presenting an absurd non-sequitur as received wisdom. Works because of her earnest delivery but the joke is slight on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Your belly is like a drum. I can feel the baby kicking in there.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's like bongo drums. Do do do do do!

jokes.text: I'm so pregnant that my guitar doesn't fit anymore, so I'm going to play my songs on this drum. It sounds really cool!
jokes.setup: Phoebe can't play guitar due to her pregnant belly.
jokes.punchline: Her solution is to play a hand drum — and she's delighted with herself after only one hour of practice.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's breezy practicality and instant self-satisfaction are perfectly in character. The 'only been playing for an hour' tag adds a nice extra beat of oblivious confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't play guitar anymore because of my belly. So I'm just gonna use it as a drum instead.

jokes.text: Phoebe performs 'Smelly Cat' on the hand drum — it sounds rhythmically odd but she's thrilled.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has switched to drum because guitar no longer fits her belly.
jokes.punchline: She plays the iconic 'Smelly Cat' on a hand drum, clearly sounding wrong, but declares it 'really cool.'
jokes.explanation: The recontextualization of 'Smelly Cat' on an unexpected instrument is a satisfying callback gag. Audience recognition of the song elevates the laugh beyond the joke's basic construction.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Smelly cat, smelly cat, what are they feeding you?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Smelly cat, smelly cat, it's not your fault.

jokes.text: Don't tell me you want to keep more stuff in my uterus.
jokes.setup: Frank Jr. arrives and says he has a big favor to ask.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately assumes the worst — that he wants her to carry more babies — referencing her surrogacy situation with weary resignation.
jokes.explanation: Economical, character-specific, and genuinely surprising. The specificity of 'more stuff in my uterus' rather than 'more babies' is sharp writing — it treats her uterus as a storage unit, which is both absurd and logical given her situation. High quotability, strong craft.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's actually really impressive.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Thanks! I've only been doing it for like twenty minutes and I'm already really good at it.

jokes.text: Frank Jr., Jr. — Wouldn't that be Frank III? / Don't get me started.
jokes.setup: Frank wants to name one boy Frank Jr., Jr.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe correctly notes that's actually Frank III; Frank's 'Don't get me started' implies he's already lost this argument and is exhausted by it.
jokes.explanation: Clean little joke with a good two-beat structure. 'Don't get me started' is a compact payoff that implies a whole offscreen argument. Economical and smart.

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr. Jr.
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I need to ask you a favor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! You want me to be a surrogate again!

jokes.text: That's so nice! Cougar.
jokes.setup: Frank and Alice ask Phoebe to name the third baby, saying it would be a great honor.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe is genuinely touched — then immediately blurts 'Cougar' as her name suggestion.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat misdirection. 'That's so nice!' sets up warmth and sentimentality; 'Cougar' demolishes it with one word. The brevity is the entire joke — it needs nothing else. Fully Phoebe-specific: only she would name a baby Cougar with zero irony. The pause beat ('Think about it') elevates it further.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. If you're Frank Senior, and he's Frank Junior, wouldn't he be Frank... the Third?

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm the Junior.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Right, but you're not Senior, so...

dialogue.speaker: Frank Jr.
dialogue.line: I'll be Senior by then.

jokes.text: Think about it. (beat)
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just proposed 'Cougar' as a baby name.
jokes.punchline: She adds 'Think about it' with complete sincerity, as if Cougar is a name that merits serious consideration.
jokes.explanation: The tag beat to Cougar. Two words that extend the laugh through Phoebe's utter earnestness. Works as a callback extension — the confidence is funnier than the name itself.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm so honored you want me to name the baby!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have the perfect name: Cougar.

jokes.text: I left a bra drying in there. Will your son think it's yours and be traumatized? Mommy can have a wife. Daddy can have a bra.
jokes.setup: Ross is at Carol and Susan's apartment; there's a bra drying somewhere visible. Carol worries about Ben seeing it.
jokes.punchline: Susan delivers a wry retort normalizing the unconventional family setup while gently jabbing at the awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: Decent joke that plays on the show's running dynamic. The parallel structure ('Mommy can have a wife / Daddy can have a bra') is tidy, but the joke itself isn't particularly sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, he'll figure it out. I mean, he sees Carol and Susan together all the time. He knows that Carol is his mother and Susan is her... partner.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So when he sees a bra, he's not going to think it's some big mystery. He'll just think, 'Oh, that's Carol's bra. Or Susan's bra.'

jokes.text: What can we do in 17 minutes... twice? Well, that's ambitious.
jokes.setup: Carol notes the clock is fast and they have 17 minutes before they need to leave.
jokes.punchline: Susan suggests sexual activity — twice — in that window; Carol calls it 'ambitious.'
jokes.explanation: 'Twice' is a solid punchline add-on, and 'that's ambitious' is a good dry response. Standard sitcom innuendo — functional but not elevated.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We still have time for a little... you know.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Ross, that's very optimistic. For you.

jokes.text: You can ignore that. That's your son. Believe me, when he's older, he'll understand.
jokes.setup: The doorbell rings interrupting an intimate moment; it's Ben (Ross's son).
jokes.punchline: Susan tells Ross to ignore his own kid at the door, then reassures him Ben will understand — implying understanding that his parents were having sex.
jokes.explanation: Susan's breezy disregard for Ross's paternal instincts is in character and mildly funny. The implication about Ben 'understanding' is the dark punchline. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Ben! What are you doing up?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I had a bad dream.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Well, you can sleep in our bed tonight.

jokes.text: It's just us getting along is difficult for him... because he doesn't like me. / Come on. That's... / It's true.
jokes.setup: Ross is visibly uncomfortable watching Carol and Susan bond with Emily. Susan calls it out.
jokes.punchline: Ross starts to deny it but can't finish the sentence, and Susan's flat 'It's true' lands as a deadpan confirmation.
jokes.explanation: Ross's inability to finish his denial is the real joke — a reaction beat made verbal. Susan's 'It's true' is drily confident. Solid character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Emily and Susan really hit it off.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Well, let's be honest, Ross. You don't like me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I don't like you.

jokes.text: You know? Like... Exxon! / It certainly worked for that Valdez kid.
jokes.setup: Phoebe wants a strong, confident baby name and builds up to it.
jokes.punchline: She suggests 'Exxon'; Joey tags with a reference to the Exxon Valdez oil spill disaster — the 'Valdez kid' implying it was a person.
jokes.explanation: Two-stage joke that works well: Phoebe's left-field corporate baby name is funny on its own, but Joey's dark Valdez tag elevates it significantly. The deadpan delivery of a reference to an environmental disaster as a child-naming success story is genuinely subversive for network TV.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Exxon. That's a strong name for a corporation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, unless you're an Alaskan fisherman.

jokes.text: You want a strong name? How about The Hulk?
jokes.setup: Everyone is brainstorming strong baby names.
jokes.punchline: Joey suggests The Hulk — a comic book character — with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Very Joey — the character's child-like pop culture frame of reference as naming criterion. Brief and punchy. Sets up a running gag through the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? I got a great name for a baby boy: Hercules.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: All the kids in school would be like, 'Hey, Hercules!' and then they'd be like, 'Yeah?'

jokes.text: I'm not sure about Hulk, but I like a name starting with 'The'.
jokes.setup: Joey suggests The Hulk as a baby name.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe doesn't reject the absurdity — she just has a minor grammatical preference: she likes names beginning with 'The.'
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's response perfectly escalates the absurdity — she doesn't reject 'The Hulk' as a concept, just the specific word 'Hulk.' Her criteria for naming a baby is the article 'The.' Pure Phoebe logic and very funny. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You could be The Hulk!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: The Hulk? I don't know... I'm not really a 'The' kind of girl.

jokes.text: You want a good name, go with Joey. Joey's your pal, your buddy. Where is everybody? They're hanging out with Joey!
jokes.setup: Everyone is debating baby names.
jokes.punchline: Joey campaigns for his own name as the best baby name, delivering a full pitch about how great 'Joey' is — referring to himself in the third person.
jokes.explanation: Joey's oblivious self-promotion is fully in character. The third-person advocacy ('Where is everybody? They're hanging out with Joey!') shows the writers using his narcissism as the actual joke rather than just having him be dumb.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna go out there and sell myself. I'm a good-looking guy, I'm a talented actor, and I'm a genuinely nice person.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How could they not want me? Joey Tribbiani - he's not just an actor, he's a force of nature! He lights up every room he walks into. Women want him, men want to BE him!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And the best part? He works cheap!

jokes.text: If you're going to name him Joey, you should name him Chandler. Chandler's funny, sophisticated, and very lovable... once you get to know him.
jokes.setup: Joey campaigns for his own name; Chandler counters by campaigning for his own name.
jokes.punchline: 'Once you get to know him' — the qualifier undercuts Chandler's whole pitch, acknowledging his off-putting personality.
jokes.explanation: The self-deprecating qualifier 'once you get to know him' is the real joke — Chandler accidentally reveals his own social liabilities while trying to sell himself. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more... Chandler? I mean, what if I went by a different name? Like, what if I was 'Brad'? Brad Bing. No, that doesn't work. What about 'Steve'? Steve Bing. See, the thing is, I've tried to distance myself from the name Chandler my whole life, but it's like this weird, awkward thing that just... it's me. I'm Chandler Bing. That IS my name. That's who I am. And I can't escape it, even though it sounds like something from a Dickens novel written by someone who had a stroke.

jokes.text: Chandler will be there too. He might be a little late... but he'll be there. And he'll bring you cold soda... if what you need him for is that you're really hot.
jokes.setup: Joey says if you need him, he'll be there. Chandler tries to match the endorsement for himself.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's version of 'being there' degrades rapidly — he'll be late, and his version of help is cold soda specifically if you're overheated.
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of Chandler's very modest offer — arriving late, bringing soda, and only if you're specifically hot — is a good descending comedy structure. His sad self-awareness makes it charming.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget all that. I think you should be a superhero whose only power is that he can turn into a big pile of wet leaves.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Phoebe...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no, hear me out! And when he does, all the bad guys just jump in the pile because it's so fun!

jokes.text: Joey and Chandler are both great names.
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler have been campaigning for their own names; Phoebe has heard the whole argument.
jokes.punchline: She dismisses both their pitches with the same noncommittal endorsement, rendering the argument pointless.
jokes.explanation: A capper beat that deflates the boys' entire argument efficiently. Not a big laugh, but good structural function.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm gonna use The Hulk on you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no! I was seriously considering that for my kid!

jokes.text: All right, I don't... Maybe I'll just name him The Hulk.
jokes.setup: Neither Joey nor Chandler has persuaded Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: She circles back to The Hulk as a genuine front-runner, keeping the absurd option alive.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that shows Phoebe is still seriously considering The Hulk. Sets up the Chandler/Hulk running gag for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So which outfit do you think is better for my date?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, you want me to choose? That's like asking me to pick a favorite child. Except your children are both ugly.

jokes.text: I shouldn't have mentioned it. I wanted to name my kid that.
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she might name the baby The Hulk.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he planned to name his own future child The Hulk — and genuinely regrets bringing it up now that competition exists.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Joey was saving The Hulk for his own kid is perfectly absurd and deeply in character. His genuine frustration that Phoebe might take 'his' name is the best part.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel's idea of cooking is putting a potato in the microwave and calling it a meal.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's not just a potato, it's a *baked* potato. And I pair it with a Diet Coke for balance.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's not balance, that's a cry for help.

jokes.text: If you hoped to sleep with Joshua, which one would you wear? / It creeps me out choosing other people's sex clothes.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks Monica to help pick an outfit, clearly wanting to impress Joshua.
jokes.punchline: Monica's blunt refusal — 'It creeps me out choosing other people's sex clothes' — is a funny deflation of the euphemism Rachel was dancing around.
jokes.explanation: 'Sex clothes' is a good, specific, slightly crude phrase that lands because it cuts through Rachel's coyness. Decent joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know, I think the problem is that Rachel doesn't really take cooking seriously.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's not true! I take it very seriously. I'm just not very good at it.

jokes.text: What am I making him, by the way? / [Monica lists an elaborate gourmet menu] / I thought I was making him filet mignon.
jokes.setup: Rachel has been hyping the fancy dinner she's cooking for Joshua.
jokes.punchline: She doesn't even know what's on the menu — Monica planned it; and when she thought it was filet mignon, Monica corrects her: she changed it to leftover salmon.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Rachel has no idea what she's supposedly 'cooking' is a good character beat — her obliviousness and Monica's control-freak planning colliding neatly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: They're doing everything together. They went to a museum, they went shopping, they went to lunch...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: They're talking about interior design! Emily's showing her fabric swatches!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Susan is laughing at her jokes. They're exchanging phone numbers!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh God, they're bonding. They're actually bonding!

jokes.text: Then you realized if you bitched, then you would stop cooking... and you would have to make your famous baked potato and Diet Coke.
jokes.setup: Monica explains why Rachel accepted the leftover salmon plan.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's alternative to Monica's cooking is a 'famous' baked potato and Diet Coke — the most pathetically minimal 'meal' imaginable.
jokes.explanation: The word 'famous' applied to a baked potato and Diet Coke is the joke — it implies Rachel has somehow built a reputation for the laziest possible meal. Good character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's always saying things like, 'Oh, Susan's so smart, Susan's so funny, Susan's so talented.' And I'm thinking, 'Yeah, well, Susan's not here anymore, Carol. Susan's gone!' But does she listen? No! It's 'Susan this' and 'Susan that.' I can't compete with Susan! Nobody can compete with Susan!

jokes.text: I really get crabby when I cook.
jokes.setup: Monica has just explained that Rachel basically outsourced the entire dinner to her.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's self-assessment — that she 'gets crabby when she cooks' — is her only explanation for this dynamic, delivered as a simple fact.
jokes.explanation: Very economical — one sentence that perfectly captures Rachel's spoiled obliviousness. The understatement implies she barely even cooks at all, let alone well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Emily and Susan at the gym together... they're on the StairMaster next to each other, and they're talking about me.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And then Emily says, 'You know, Susan, Ross is really—' and Susan interrupts her and says, 'I know, he's very—'

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And then they're both on the StairMaster and they're both looking at me, and they're both—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like that scene in Jaws, you know? When all the women realize there's a shark in the water? That's what this is like. Except I'm the shark.

jokes.text: So Emily called last night. / And now you're giving me the message?
jokes.setup: Ross mentions Emily called, clearly expecting this is relevant information.
jokes.punchline: Joey's incredulous response implies Ross sat on the message until now — a classic Joey self-centeredness beat.
jokes.explanation: Quick joke that works as a character beat — Joey's immediate instinct is about himself (the message should have come to him sooner). Brief but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Personal Best? Dude, I gotta see that!

jokes.text: They're going to the theater together. They're going to dinner. They're going horseback riding! God, Susan is so fun!
jokes.setup: Ross explains what Emily and Susan have been doing in London.
jokes.punchline: The list keeps escalating — theater, dinner, horseback riding — until Ross breaks and can only say 'God, Susan is so fun!' with begrudging, agonized admiration.
jokes.explanation: Ross's involuntary compliment about his nemesis is the payoff — the escalating activities make his suffering clear before the punchline admission. Good Ross character work: his jealousy of Susan is longstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I just want to make sure we pick the right name for the baby.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I have some thoughts on that. 'Ross' is a terrible name for a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? That's my name!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Exactly. It sounds like a name someone made up when they ran out of real names. Like, 'We need a name... Ross! Done.'

jokes.text: For six months before Carol and I split up, all I heard was 'My friend Susan is so smart. My friend Susan is so funny. My friend Susan is so great.'
jokes.setup: Ross explains his anxiety about Emily bonding with Susan.
jokes.punchline: He lists the compliments Carol used to give Susan — revealing he was clearly tortured by this catalog of praise while his marriage was collapsing.
jokes.explanation: Good backstory comedy — the specificity of the repeated praise pattern reveals the psychological wound underneath Ross's paranoia. Character-specific to both Ross and his history with Susan/Carol.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm having an emotional crisis and you're upset about my name?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Your name is Ross!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know my name is Ross.

jokes.text: You think something could happen between Emily and Susan? Hey, they're going to the gym together! / Two women... stretching! They take a steam, things get playful. Didn't you see 'Personal Best'?
jokes.setup: Ross wonders if Emily might be attracted to Susan.
jokes.punchline: Joey fills in the fantasy with absurd specificity — steam room, stretching, 'things get playful' — and references an actual lesbian film ('Personal Best') as evidence.
jokes.explanation: Joey's cinematic knowledge of lesbian films as evidence for a real-world concern is both in character and funny. The escalating specificity ('things get playful') is well constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why does everyone else get to be happy? Monica has Chandler, Rachel has... well, she's working on it. Even Phoebe found someone. And me? I'm stuck being... being...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What, like a superhero? 'Captain Dateless'?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, exactly. Except Captain Dateless actually has a cool name.

jokes.text: No, but I'm gonna!
jokes.setup: Joey references 'Personal Best' as evidence Emily and Susan might hook up; Ross hasn't seen it.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately commits to watching it — not out of skepticism but perhaps to research his anxiety, or because it suddenly sounds relevant.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words that reveal Ross is now fully aboard the paranoid fantasy spiral. The speed of his commitment is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, if you look at the comic book canon, Spider-Man's web fluid has a tensile strength of—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget it. I can't believe Rachel is dating Paolo.

jokes.text: Hi! You're crazy. Emily is straight. How do you know? We thought Carol was straight.
jokes.setup: Ross is spiraling about Emily and Susan; Chandler tries to dismiss it.
jokes.punchline: Ross's rebuttal — 'We thought Carol was straight' — is devastating and unanswerable. It lands because it's true.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'We thought Carol was straight' is perfectly constructed — it's Ross's most humiliating biographical fact weaponized as logical evidence. Chandler's 'Hi! You're crazy' opener also adds comic rhythm. The structure (assertion → challenge → unanswerable comeback) is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There are no famous Joeys.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, there was Joey Buttafuoco.

jokes.text: Yeah, definitely. I don't like the name Ross.
jokes.setup: Ross is having an emotional moment about his girlfriend potentially being gay.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe abruptly shifts to her baby-naming deliberations — dismissing 'Ross' as a name option mid-crisis, completely ignoring Ross's distress.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant tonal whiplash. Phoebe's complete obliviousness to Ross's crisis and her timing — 'Yeah, definitely' agreeing with... nothing — before rejecting his name for the baby is perfectly absurd. The fact that she's essentially insulting his name to his face without noticing makes it even better.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What about Chandler Joey? Or Joandler? Pheeandler? Wait, that's me.

jokes.text: What a weird way to kick me when I'm down!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just said she doesn't like the name 'Ross' — to Ross's face — in the middle of his emotional crisis.
jokes.punchline: Ross's wounded reaction — 'What a weird way to kick me when I'm down!' — before Phoebe clarifies she meant for the baby.
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure with the clarification ('No, I meant for the baby') makes this a mini callback. Ross's specific word choice — 'weird way to kick me when I'm down' — is funny because he's right, it IS a weird way. Good reaction comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more qualified to be president?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you'd have to actually run for office first.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I've run from things my whole life. How is this different?

jokes.text: Something like this would never happen to The Hulk, you know. / That's not true. In 'The Incredible Hulk', number 72, Dr. Bruce Banner found... / You know what, never mind. My girlfriend's a lesbian.
jokes.setup: Ross is spiraling about Emily; Joey tries to comfort with Hulk lore.
jokes.punchline: Joey begins citing a specific comic book issue where Bruce Banner DID face a similar problem — before Ross cuts him off with resigned despair: 'My girlfriend's a lesbian.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Three things work simultaneously: (1) The Hulk callback pays off; (2) Joey's specific comic issue citation implies The Hulk DID face romantic trouble, which is absurdly specific; (3) Ross's resignation — 'never mind, my girlfriend's a lesbian' — is a perfect deflation that brings the meta-absurdity crashing back to his real pain. The construction is excellent: setup, surprising counter-argument, devastating reversal. 'My girlfriend's a lesbian' as Ross's conclusion is the best punchline in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, okay. 'Chandler'? What kind of name is Chandler? It sounds like you should be working in a department store or something. 'Can I help you find some slacks?' No! It's a terrible name!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's not that bad.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Not that bad?! It's worse than bad! You know what your name sounds like? A candle maker. A guy who makes candles!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, that's what it means.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Exactly! Why would your parents name you after a job? That's insane! I mean, at least my name is cool. Joey Tribbiani — that's a name with style, with pizzazz!

jokes.text: Name one famous person named Chandler. / Raymond Chandler. / Someone you didn't make up.
jokes.setup: Joey challenges Chandler to name a famous 'Chandler.' Chandler correctly identifies Raymond Chandler, the famous novelist.
jokes.punchline: Joey dismisses Raymond Chandler as someone Chandler 'made up' — revealing his complete ignorance of one of the most famous American crime writers.
jokes.explanation: Superb economy and character integration. Joey's confident dismissal of Raymond Chandler as a fabrication is simultaneously a great Joey stupidity joke AND a great structural joke about the name debate. The beat works because Chandler's answer is completely correct — he is vindicated — and then immediately dismissed. 'Someone you didn't make up' is a quotable, memorable line.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more pathetic?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I could try.

jokes.text: There are no famous Joeys. Except for... Joey Buttafucco. / Yeah, that guy really hurt us.
jokes.setup: Chandler argues back that there are no famous Joeys.
jokes.punchline: He cites Joey Buttafucco (the notorious tabloid figure); Joey agrees solemnly that 'that guy really hurt us' — as if he represents all Joeys.
jokes.explanation: Joey's earnest tribal solidarity with an infamous tabloid figure — 'that guy really hurt us' — is perfectly absurd and in character. The reference is specific enough to be sharp without being obscure for its era.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua
dialogue.line: What the—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, don't worry about them. They come every year around this time.

jokes.text: How about a compromise then? What if it's... Chan-no-ey? / Joey? Think about it. He'll never be President. There will never be a President Joey.
jokes.setup: Joey and Chandler can't agree on a name; Chandler proposes a portmanteau.
jokes.punchline: 'Chan-no-ey' is a terrible portmanteau; Joey rejects it and counters by arguing 'Joey' disqualifies the child from the presidency — which is oddly specific and arguably correct.
jokes.explanation: 'Chan-no-ey' is funny on its own as a terrible name. Joey's presidential electability argument is unexpectedly specific and implies he has thought about this seriously — good character beat. 'There will never be a President Joey' is a memorable line.

jokes.text: Chandler is the stupidest name I've heard in my life! It's not a name! It's barely even a word. It's like chandelier but it's not!
jokes.setup: Joey finally drops the diplomatic pretense and attacks the name Chandler directly.
jokes.punchline: 'It's like chandelier but it's not!' — Joey's linguistic analysis reveals he sees Chandler as an incomplete chandelier, which is both insulting and oddly poetic.
jokes.explanation: Escalating outrage that peaks at genuine absurdist insight: Chandler is not a chandelier. The logic is completely Joey — he's tried to dissect the word and arrived at something that sounds both stupid and weirdly correct. 'It's like chandelier but it's not' is the standout line and genuinely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua
dialogue.line: Look, I know what you're all thinking. But it's not irrational! Birds are unpredictable. They have those beady little eyes, and they move so fast you can't see where they're going. Plus, have you ever really looked at their feet? They're like tiny alien claws!

jokes.text: You're right. I have a horrible, horrible name.
jokes.setup: Joey has gone on a prolonged rant about how terrible 'Chandler' is as a name.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, crushed, quietly agrees — the double 'horrible' suggesting the name has broken through his defenses and he now fully accepts its awfulness.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical deflation. Chandler's complete capitulation after his spirited self-defense is funny precisely because it's so total. 'Horrible, horrible' is the right intensifier — not 'terrible' but 'horrible' twice.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, they're birds, Joshua. They fly. It probably only takes them like, what, twenty minutes?

jokes.text: So I guess it's Joey then.
jokes.setup: Chandler has conceded his name is horrible; Joey has won by attrition.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe matter-of-factly concludes the debate has been settled — but only because Chandler gave up, not because Joey made any good argument.
jokes.explanation: Functional capper beat that closes the naming argument. Not particularly funny on its own but serves the scene structure.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The birds will just peck their way back out.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua
dialogue.line: That's not funny.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. / I know. My God, this rice is so— / I am so good!
jokes.setup: Rachel and Joshua sit down to eat the elaborate dinner Monica cooked.
jokes.punchline: Monica interjects her own self-congratulation — 'I am so good!' — as Rachel and Joshua begin complimenting the food, reminding us this isn't Rachel's cooking at all.
jokes.explanation: Monica's inability to resist self-congratulation from across the room — crashing Rachel's romantic moment — is a good character beat. Tells us Rachel's charade is about to get complicated.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He's like a nature documentary. 'And here we see the male bird in his natural habitat, nervously preening his feathers, unaware that the female is about to reject him.'

jokes.text: Behind you. / [Chickens/ducks appear] They used to live here, and sometimes they migrate back over. / Farm birds really kind of freak me out!
jokes.setup: Rachel's romantic dinner is interrupted by Monica's appearance. Then Joshua reveals something unexpected about himself.
jokes.punchline: Joey and Chandler's pet duck/chicken wander into the apartment; Joshua is terrified of 'farm birds,' destroying the romantic mood.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of the birds wandering in mid-romantic-dinner is a solid visual gag. Joshua's specific phobia ('farm birds') is an absurd character detail that recontextualizes the cute duck/chicken recurring element. 'They migrate back over' as an explanation is a good Monica deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: So what did you do today, Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Did you play with your toys?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Did you watch TV?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, you must be dead.

jokes.text: It's just that I know that they're still out there. / They're across the hall. That's two doors away. It'll take them a long time to peck their way back over here. / That's not funny.
jokes.setup: Joshua can't relax because the birds are nearby. Rachel tries to reassure him with a quip about how long it would take birds to 'peck their way back.'
jokes.punchline: Joshua's flat 'That's not funny' — delivered with zero humor — shows his phobia is real and Rachel's joke has fallen completely flat, escalating the awkwardness.
jokes.explanation: 'Peck their way back over here' is a good line from Rachel; Joshua shutting it down with 'That's not funny' is a cringe beat that works. The comedy is Rachel's discomfort at her joke bombing on her date.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, their marriage was a loving, committed relationship too.

jokes.text: They can smell the fear.
jokes.setup: Joshua is terrified of the birds; Rachel has been trying to manage the situation.
jokes.punchline: Rachel mutters 'They can smell the fear' — applying predator logic to the apartment duck and chicken.
jokes.explanation: Very economical — applying a predator-fear metaphor to apartment birds is funny. Brief and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm starting to think Susan might be right about Emily...

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I've convinced myself.

jokes.text: I asked if he wanted to eat. He said no. I asked if he wanted to sleep. He said no. I asked what he wanted to do. He said no. So he's sweeping.
jokes.setup: Ross checks in on Ben; Carol asks how he's doing.
jokes.punchline: After listing Ben's string of 'no' answers to everything, the punchline is that the logical conclusion was: sweeping. Ben is toddler-sweeping because Ross ran out of options.
jokes.explanation: The list structure is perfectly executed: three questions with 'no,' leading to the absurd but logical answer of sweeping. It's a parenting joke that earns the punchline through the rhythm of the setup. 'So he's sweeping' is a great final beat.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: When I was a kid, a duck chased me. I couldn't have been more than seven. It was the most traumatic thing that ever happened to me.

jokes.text: What's too much fun? / The kind of fun you and Susan had when we were married.
jokes.setup: Ross implies Emily and Susan might be having 'too much fun.' Carol asks what 'too much fun' means.
jokes.punchline: Ross's answer — 'The kind of fun you and Susan had when we were married' — is a perfect blade: pointing out that Carol and Susan's affair began while they were still married.
jokes.explanation: Ross lands a genuinely devastating line. 'The kind of fun you and Susan had when we were married' is both funny and cutting — it acknowledges the affair and uses it as logical evidence. The structure (definition through personal example) is tight. Carol's silent reaction is the visual punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Was the fancy house a babe magnet growing up?

dialogue.speaker: Joshua
dialogue.line: Well, I didn't grow up in that house. My parents bought it after I was in college.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua
dialogue.line: But speaking of babe magnets, how many guys have you gone through since college?

jokes.text: They're coming back from the theater, and they stop at a pub for drinks. They're laughing. Someone innocently touches someone else. There's electricity. It's new. It's exciting.
jokes.setup: Ross is building the case that Susan might seduce Emily.
jokes.punchline: Ross's cinematic reconstruction of the imagined seduction becomes increasingly romantic-novel-specific ('there's electricity... it's new... it's exciting'), revealing how vividly and obsessively he's imagined this scenario.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the specificity and passion of Ross's anxiety-fantasy. His romance-novel cadence reveals he's thought about this in vivid romantic terms, which is both pathetic and funny. The escalation works.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's Mother
dialogue.line: Well, we're back from France.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's Father
dialogue.line: Dreadful place.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's Mother
dialogue.line: Absolutely dreadful.

jokes.text: Are you saying there isn't the slightest possibility of something happening? / Maybe. / Oh, my God! I didn't really believe it until you just said it!
jokes.setup: Ross presses Carol to admit there's zero possibility of Susan seducing Emily.
jokes.punchline: Carol hedges with 'Maybe' — meaning maybe there's a slight possibility — and Ross treats this as full confirmation of his paranoia.
jokes.explanation: The trap Ross walks into — pushing Carol for certainty and getting just enough ambiguity to validate his fears — is well constructed. 'I didn't really believe it until you just said it' is an excellent punchline because Ross acknowledges his own irrationality while being completely unable to stop it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can also cook, clean, and do laundry!

jokes.text: None of the other kids believed me, but I swear that duck pushed me.
jokes.setup: Scene cuts to Ben (a toddler) apparently relating a story.
jokes.punchline: A toddler gravely insisting, with the seriousness of an adult, that a duck pushed him — and that the other kids didn't believe him.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny kid line delivered with straight-faced adult gravity. 'None of the other kids believed me' is the perfect setup for a toddler — giving him the full credibility-defense of a grown witness. The duck callback connects to Joey's pet. High quotability and genuine charm.

jokes.text: This is the downstairs living room. / There's two living rooms? / Growing up here, this place must have been a real babe magnet. / It would have been, but my parents just moved here.
jokes.setup: Rachel shows Joshua her parents' house, mentioning it's the 'downstairs living room.' Joshua asks if she grew up here.
jokes.punchline: Rachel has apparently been implying she grew up in this mansion to impress Joshua — but it falls apart when she admits her parents 'just moved here.'
jokes.explanation: Rachel's failed attempt at impression-management is a good character beat. The reveal that her 'childhood home' pitch collapses instantly is a neat little structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's father
dialogue.line: Did my son buy you that outfit?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes, he did.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's father
dialogue.line: That must have cost a fortune. Where'd he get the money?

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's father
dialogue.line: Please tell me that's not the grocery money.

jokes.text: You should know this place is a real babe magnet.
jokes.setup: Her 'I grew up here' story has just been debunked.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately pivots — she can't use the childhood angle, so she just promotes the house's current attractiveness directly.
jokes.explanation: Quick callback that works as a character beat — Rachel's flexibility in self-promotion is funny. Not a big laugh but good rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, so I was helping out at this really important photo shoot for a major fashion designer...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And they needed someone to model the clothes, so I volunteered because, you know, it's fashion.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: But then the designer said my regular clothes weren't... fashion-forward enough, so they gave me this outfit to wear instead.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's actually very expensive. It's a limited edition piece that most people can't even pull off.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Plus, I got paid! Well, I mean, I will get paid. Once the check clears. From the fashion people.

jokes.text: Hi, darling. / What are you doing here? / We cut the trip short. / France sucks!
jokes.setup: Rachel has finally gotten Joshua alone in the romantic, empty house.
jokes.punchline: Her parents arrive home early. Her father's reason: 'France sucks!' — a gloriously petulant excuse from a presumably wealthy man.
jokes.explanation: 'France sucks!' is a punchy, specific punchline with a great comic register — the entitled dismissal of an entire country. The interruption itself is a classic sitcom structure, executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I think America is ready.

jokes.text: Hi, you! / Oh, my God!
jokes.setup: Rachel has gone to change. The implication is she's put on something revealing to seduce Joshua. She emerges.
jokes.punchline: Joshua's 'Oh, my God!' reaction — combined with Rachel's confident 'I know. I can do more than cook' — implies the dress/outfit is extremely provocative. This is a visual gag: the audience sees what Joshua sees.
jokes.explanation: The visual gag is the reveal of Rachel's outfit (the 'new dress' of the episode title). Impact depends heavily on the visual; the dialogue alone is merely functional setup.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's father
dialogue.line: You know, that's a very nice outfit. It would be a shame to waste it.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's father
dialogue.line: Why don't you go seduce my son?

jokes.text: I like her. She seems smart.
jokes.setup: Rachel's father has just watched Rachel walk in wearing an apparently scandalous outfit while trying to seduce Joshua.
jokes.punchline: His verdict: 'She seems smart.' — delivered with either sincere misreading of the situation or perfectly deadpan irony.
jokes.explanation: Very economical and plays well on ironic ambiguity — is he being obtuse or sarcastic? Either way it's funny. 'She seems smart' as a non sequitur response to whatever Rachel is wearing is a sharp punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Joshua's Mother
dialogue.line: Well, I can see you're not wearing much under that dress.

jokes.text: Joshua, that $500 was for groceries.
jokes.setup: Rachel's mother meets Rachel and seems to have given Joshua money previously — but sees how it was spent.
jokes.punchline: The $500 Rachel apparently spent (presumably on the provocative outfit) was intended for groceries — a stunning misallocation that reveals Rachel's priorities.
jokes.explanation: $500 for a dress when given grocery money is a good character-specific joke about Rachel's relationship with money and priorities. Brief, economical, well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more insulted? That's it. From now on, I'm going by my middle name. I'm Muriel now.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Muriel?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's right. Muriel Bing. Has a nice ring to it, don't you think?

jokes.text: What, this? Oh, no. That's not what it is. Okay, I work in fashion. And this is a real dress, actually. They're wearing it in Milan. Part of my job is to wear the clothes and see how people respond. Then I report back to my superiors at Bloomingdale's.
jokes.setup: Rachel's parents are clearly scandalized by her outfit. She needs to explain.
jokes.punchline: Rachel spins an elaborate lie about her outfit being a professional 'field test' for Bloomingdale's — essentially claiming she's wearing something scandalous as market research.
jokes.explanation: The increasingly elaborate cover story is a good cringe comedy sequence. 'Report back to my superiors at Bloomingdale's' is an excellent, specific phrase that makes the lie sound both credible and absurd. Rachel's desperation reads through the escalating detail.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So your name is just Chandler Chandler?

jokes.text: Obviously, in this case... I am going to report back: 'U.S.A. Not ready.' / Maybe in L.A.
jokes.setup: Rachel has been spinning the 'market research for Bloomingdale's' story.
jokes.punchline: She concludes her 'report' would be that the U.S. is not ready for this look; her father helpfully suggests L.A. might be — playing along with the absurd fiction.
jokes.explanation: 'U.S.A. Not ready' is a great, clipped corporate-speak punchline. The father's earnest 'Maybe in L.A.' tag extends it nicely — suggesting he's either gullible or gently playing along.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I need a new first name. Something more masculine.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What about Clint?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Clint? That's perfect! Clint Bing. I'm gonna be a whole new man.

jokes.text: No use wasting this baby just lying around the house. / So we'll go eat. You'll wear that. We'll be eating and, of course, you'll be wearing that.
jokes.setup: Rachel's father has offered to take everyone to dinner. Her mother starts commenting on the outfit.
jokes.punchline: The mother's repeated insistence on noting — 'you'll be wearing that' and 'of course, you'll be wearing that' — escalates into barely-concealed horror at the idea of appearing in public with Rachel in this dress.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'you'll be wearing that' is a solid escalation joke. The rhythm of the line builds the cringe effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No way! You can't pull off 'Chandler.' You gotta go with 'Gene.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Gene? Why Gene?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Because that's the only name you could pull off.

jokes.text: I am sorry about what I said. / Nope, you're right. It is a ridiculous name! / It's not bad. / Yes, it is! From now on, I have no first name.
jokes.setup: Joey apologizes for his rant about the name Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Instead of accepting the apology, Chandler doubles down — 'It is a ridiculous name!' — and then declares he has no first name anymore.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's overcorrection — going from defending his name to fully disowning it — is good character comedy. The spiral continues nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I'm Chandler now!

jokes.text: You're just Bing?
jokes.setup: Chandler says he has no first name anymore.
jokes.punchline: Joey's first instinct is that this makes Chandler 'just Bing' — which is somehow even worse than Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words. 'Just Bing' is somehow a funnier, sadder name than Chandler, and Joey's matter-of-fact delivery of this worst-case scenario is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Her casual self-assessment after the wardrobe malfunction

jokes.text: So what are we supposed to call you? / Okay, for now, temporarily, you can call me... Clint.
jokes.setup: Chandler has renounced his first name.
jokes.punchline: His replacement name is 'Clint' — a name he has clearly chosen for maximum coolness, delivered with notable self-seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's choice of 'Clint' is perfect — it's exactly what an insecure person would choose as a 'cool' replacement name. The hedging ('for now, temporarily') makes it even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're saying poetry is... gay?

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: No, Ross, not all poetry is gay.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But some of it is, right? Because that's what I'm hearing.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Oh my God, no. We just went to see a poem about nature.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Nature? That's very... suspicious.

jokes.text: No way are you cool enough to pull off 'Clint'. / What name am I cool enough to pull off? / Gene.
jokes.setup: Chandler has chosen 'Clint' as his new name.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shuts down 'Clint' immediately, and when asked what he could pull off, she offers: 'Gene.' Not a cool name. A very uncool name.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup (Chandler can't pull off Clint) creates expectation that Phoebe will offer a cooler alternative. The punchline — 'Gene' — is devastating because it's the least cool name imaginable, delivered flatly with zero self-awareness. The structure is perfect: challenge → escalation → brutal deflation. 'Gene' as a single-word punchline is excellent comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: She completely changed him. He used to be so funny and now he's just a... a sycophant!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A sycophant?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes! Someone who changes who they are to please someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know what a sycophant is. I just don't think that's the word you're looking for.

jokes.text: It's Clint! / It's Clint! / Bye, Gene. / It's Clint!
jokes.setup: Chandler insists on being called Clint.
jokes.punchline: Everyone calls him Gene anyway; his increasingly desperate corrections ('It's Clint!') become the joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'Gene' joke has legs as a running gag and the rhythm of 'It's Clint!' corrections is satisfying. 'Bye, Gene' from Phoebe is a great exit line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're a sycophant!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I don't even know what that means.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But I'm not going to argue with the other two things you said.

jokes.text: What's up with Gene?
jokes.setup: Chandler has been insisting he's 'Clint'; Ross enters and has missed the whole thing.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately calls him 'Gene' — having apparently already absorbed the new nickname — which suggests Phoebe or Joey told him, or it's already stuck.
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag callback — Ross's casual use of 'Gene' shows the name has already won, and Chandler's battle is lost. The brevity is ideal.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so Ross has trust issues. And apparently they started when he was seven years old. So for the past... *counts on fingers* ...twenty-eight years, he's been living in Paranoid City. Population: Ross.

jokes.text: You wore your nightie to dinner? / The best part was when the waiter spilled water down my back. I jumped up and my boob popped out. / It's all right. I got nice boobs.
jokes.setup: Ross questions Rachel about wearing what appears to be a revealing dress to dinner with her parents.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's dinner was a disaster — water spilled on her back, her boob came out — but she concludes with cheerful resignation: 'It's all right. I got nice boobs.'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the dress plot is good — the dinner was a complete disaster, but Rachel's consolation ('I got nice boobs') is delivered with such self-satisfaction that it's endearing and funny. The escalation (spilled water → boob popped out → philosophical acceptance) works perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this is so much fun!

jokes.text: She and Susan are going to a poetry reading together. / So? / Poetry? Susan's gay. They're being gay together!
jokes.setup: Ross gets another update about Emily and Susan's activities in London.
jokes.punchline: Ross's logic: poetry → gayness. 'They're being gay together!' is the hysterical conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Ross's increasingly unhinged syllogism — poetry = gay = they're being gay together — is good escalating paranoia comedy. 'They're being gay together!' as a phrase is memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You can't let Carol ruin your relationship with Emily. You have to be the better version of Ross.

jokes.text: Carol really messed you up. / Excuse me? / She turned you into this untrusting, crazy, jealous... sycophant!
jokes.setup: Ross is spiraling about Emily and Susan. Monica calls him out.
jokes.punchline: 'Sycophant!' — delivered with conviction as the culminating insult, but it's the wrong word entirely for what she's describing.
jokes.explanation: The setup builds perfectly — 'untrusting, crazy, jealous' are all correct characterizations of Ross — before the punchline undercuts Monica's entire argument by using the wrong word with absolute confidence. 'Sycophant' means someone who flatters to gain favor — the opposite of what she means. The confidence of the wrong word makes it funnier than any correct insult would be.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Fine! You know what? I don't want your advice anymore. I don't want anybody's advice. From now on, I'm making all my own decisions. And I hope you're all happy when I'm miserable!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We will be.

jokes.text: So I don't know what 'sycophant' means, but the rest is right.
jokes.setup: Monica has just called Ross a 'sycophant.'
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately admits she doesn't know what it means either, but endorses everything else Monica said — a perfect double acknowledgment that neither of them knows the word but both feel its energy.
jokes.explanation: Perfect tag to the sycophant joke. Rachel's admission is both self-aware and unself-aware simultaneously — she knows she doesn't know the word, but that doesn't stop her from endorsing its use. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I need help choosing a new name.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, let's see. You're short, you're stocky, you've got that funny hair... I'd say 'Barney.'

jokes.text: When we were together, you got upset about Mark, and there was nothing.
jokes.setup: Rachel supports Monica's argument that Ross is irrationally jealous.
jokes.punchline: Rachel uses her own relationship with Ross as evidence — specifically the Mark situation, where Ross's jealousy broke them up. The irony is Rachel citing this as 'nothing' while the audience knows it destroyed their relationship.
jokes.explanation: This is a meta-joke that rewards long-term viewers — the callback to the Ross/Rachel/Mark storyline that broke the central couple apart. The comic irony of Rachel dismissing it as 'nothing' while knowing the weight it carries for the audience is rich.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm thinking Chad or Brad.

jokes.text: In high school, you weren't jealous at all... even though all your girlfriends cheated on you.
jokes.setup: Monica is building a timeline of Ross's jealousy development.
jokes.punchline: The 'even though all your girlfriends cheated on you' revelation — delivered as a simple historical fact — is a devastating detail about Ross's past that he apparently never connected to anything.
jokes.explanation: The casual insertion of 'all your girlfriends cheated on you' as a parenthetical is excellent dark comedy. It retroactively explains why Ross's jealousy makes psychological sense while undercutting his dignity. Monica's matter-of-fact delivery is crucial.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm not saying your name doesn't suck, but dude, you ARE a major problem.

jokes.text: So up until '92, '93, he was very trusting. Then '94 hit, Carol left him, and bam! Paranoid City!
jokes.setup: Monica has been diagnosing Ross's jealousy timeline.
jokes.punchline: Rachel reduces Ross's psychological history to a pop-analysis with 'bam! Paranoid City!' — treating a complex emotional breakdown like a sports commentator calling a play.
jokes.explanation: 'Paranoid City' is a great coinage. The sports-commentary register applied to a friend's psychological breakdown is funny and character-appropriate for Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more ashamed of your name?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I mean, my parents named me after a city in Massachusetts, a biblical king, and my mother's maiden name. It's like they were trying to ruin my life.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'm changing my name to Chandler. From now on, I'm Chandler Bing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because someone has to love your name, and apparently it's not going to be you.

jokes.text: This is so fun! / This is not fun!
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel are enjoying analyzing Ross's psychology; Ross is being dissected.
jokes.punchline: Monica's 'This is so fun!' directly contradicts Ross's 'This is not fun!' — the contrast between the analyzer's delight and the subject's misery is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom opposing-reaction joke. Works because the contrast is sharp and both lines are delivered simultaneously. Brief and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Emily!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Emily!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, hi!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, hi!

jokes.text: The '92 Ross wouldn't.
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel urge Ross not to let his Carol experience ruin things with Emily.
jokes.punchline: Monica invokes the idealized 'pre-trauma Ross' — 'the '92 Ross' — as a specific year-branded character he should aspire to be.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — four words that create the concept of a golden-era Ross and implicitly shame the current version. The year-branding ('the '92 Ross') is an inspired way to crystallize the timeline joke from earlier.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Ross, I'm so glad you're okay. But when you kiss me hello, please don't use your tongue.

jokes.text: I still think I was right about that Mark thing.
jokes.setup: Ross has just accepted the advice about not being paranoid with Emily.
jokes.punchline: He immediately contradicts his growth by insisting the Mark situation was justified — unable to let it go even after agreeing to do better.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character beat — Ross's one step forward, one step back dynamic is both funny and emotionally accurate. The callback to Mark gets an additional laugh from anyone following the show.

jokes.text: Well, you know what? I hope Emily is a lesbian.
jokes.setup: Ross's friends have talked him down from his Emily/Susan panic.
jokes.punchline: His parting shot — sarcastically wishing for the thing he feared — is delivered with petulant resignation.
jokes.explanation: Good petulant exit line from Ross. The ironic reversal (hoping for the feared outcome) is a solid character punchline.

jokes.text: Am I a Mark or a John?
jokes.setup: Chandler is now contemplating legally changing his name.
jokes.punchline: He's narrowed his rename options to 'Mark' or 'John' — two of the most generic possible names, the opposite of Clint.
jokes.explanation: His name crisis has evolved from 'Clint' to considering 'Mark or John' — both completely generic. The escalation of his identity crisis is good character comedy.

jokes.text: You're not tall enough to be a Mark. But you might make a good Barney.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks if he's a Mark or a John.
jokes.punchline: Joey's analysis: Marks are tall; Chandler isn't; therefore Barney. The logic is completely invented and Joey delivers it as received wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Joey's invented logic about names and height — delivered with complete confidence — is excellent Joey character comedy. 'You might make a good Barney' is a devastating downgrade even from Mark or John.

jokes.text: Tomorrow at 3:30, I'm going to the courthouse. This name has held me back my entire life. It's why kids picked on me and why I never do well with women.
jokes.setup: Chandler is treating his name change as a serious personal liberation moment.
jokes.punchline: He lists the name's supposed damage — bullying, romantic failure — attributing all his life problems to being named Chandler, which is both pathetic and funny given the audience knows his issues run much deeper.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's sincere belief that his name caused all his problems is both sympathetic and absurd. It's good character work because there's real Chandler-specific insecurity underneath the comedy.

jokes.text: So tomorrow, I'll either be Mark Johnson or John Markson.
jokes.setup: Chandler is going to change his name.
jokes.punchline: His two options are 'Mark Johnson' and 'John Markson' — essentially the same name rearranged, so anagram-adjacent mediocrity. He's not even committed to a direction.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever joke. 'Mark Johnson or John Markson' is essentially the same name reversed — Chandler's big identity reinvention is barely a reinvention at all. The wordplay is elegant and character-perfect: even when escaping his name, Chandler can't commit to anything genuinely different.

jokes.text: You've got problems because of you, not your name!
jokes.setup: Chandler blames his name for all his life problems.
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers the blunt truth — Chandler's problems are Chandler's fault — which is both a great put-down and an accidental compliment (he's not that limited by his name, he's just limited).
jokes.explanation: Joey telling the truth accidentally is a classic Joey comedy beat. 'You've got problems because of you' is accurate and devastating. The bluntness without cruelty is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: This has got to stop! Chandler is a great name. In fact... I'm sorry, I know you wanted me to name the baby Joey. I'm going to name the baby Chandler.
jokes.setup: Chandler is spiraling about his name; Phoebe has been listening.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe defends 'Chandler' as a great name — but her defense is actually a baby-naming decision. She's going to name the baby Chandler, not compliment Chandler.
jokes.explanation: Superb structural payoff. The joke has two satisfying callbacks: (1) the entire Joey vs. Chandler baby name debate is resolved, and (2) Chandler's self-loathing over his name is resolved simultaneously. Phoebe's declaration is a double misdirect — it sounds like she's defending Chandler the person, then pivots to naming the baby, then has to apologize to Joey. The construction rewards anyone who followed the whole episode.

jokes.text: Really? / But you have to keep the name too. / Okay, thanks!
jokes.setup: Phoebe names the baby Chandler, which delights Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe adds the condition: Chandler must keep his name too — removing his ability to change it. 'Okay, thanks!' is Chandler's instant, grateful acceptance.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's condition neatly closes the name-change subplot — the baby naming resolves Chandler's identity crisis by making him feel the name is worth keeping. 'Okay, thanks!' is a great punctuation. Economical and emotionally satisfying while remaining funny.

jokes.text: You want to hug it out?
jokes.setup: Chandler has had an emotional moment after Phoebe names the baby after him.
jokes.punchline: He offers to 'hug it out' — a masculine deflection of genuine emotion.
jokes.explanation: Decent tag beat that closes the scene with Chandler's characteristic emotional deflection. Light and functional.

jokes.text: Nice luggage. / I was going to say.
jokes.setup: Ross and Emily are reuniting at the airport after her trip with Susan.
jokes.punchline: Both of them notice the other's 'luggage' and exchange what are apparently loaded or ironic compliments — possibly referring to emotional baggage rather than actual luggage.
jokes.explanation: Ambiguous enough to work as a wordplay joke about emotional vs. literal luggage, or just a sweet moment. Mildly amusing but understated.

jokes.text: No tongue.
jokes.setup: Ross and Emily are having an apparently passionate reunion kiss at the airport.
jokes.punchline: An off-screen voice (Ross's mother / someone nearby) says 'No tongue' — a prude interjection that undercuts the romantic moment.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum economy, good laugh. The intrusion of a disapproving third party on a romantic moment is a classic sitcom button. 'No tongue' as the final line of the episode is a solid closing joke — brief, unexpected, and funny.

tmdb_overview: Rachel has an awkward encounter with Joshua's parents. Phoebe is offered the chance to name one of the triplets. Ross becomes paranoid when Emily goes to London with Susan.
insight: Four-minute cold open carries the episode with rapid-fire observational comedy.
